solutions.17: The terms are doubled, not increased by 3: 3 × 2 = 6, 6 × 2 = 12, 12 × 2 = 24. The next term is 24 × 2 = 48.

written.22: For each shape, give the number of lines of symmetry and the smallest angle of symmetry: equilateral triangle, square, rectangle (not a square), regular pentagon, circle.
23: A paper windmill has 4 identical blades, equally spaced.
(a) Find its smallest angle of symmetry.
(b) List all its angles of symmetry up to 360°.
(c) The blades are bent so that the windmill has no line of symmetry. Does it still have rotational symmetry? Explain.
24: (a) How many lines of symmetry does the logo have? [1]
(b) Find its smallest angle of symmetry. [1]
(c) A square replaces the triangle. How do the answers change? Which logo looks the same more times in one full turn? [2]

papers.caseStudy: A logo is a circle with an equilateral triangle inside it. The corners of the triangle are on the circle, and the triangle is not coloured differently in any part.

solutions.17: Only a square has 4. A rectangle that is not a square has 2 lines (through the mid-points of opposite sides). Its diagonals are not lines of symmetry.
solutions.18: (a) A rectangle, or a rhombus, or the letter H. (b) A parallelogram, or the letter S, or a pinwheel.
solutions.19: 0, 1 and 8 stay the same. 6 and 9 change into each other. The greatest such 4-digit number is 9966: after a half turn it reads 9966 again.
solutions.20: (a) 60°, 120°, 180°, 240°, 300° and 360°. (b) It looks the same only after a full turn, so it no longer has rotational symmetry. (c) At most 1 line (through the centre and the coloured petal).
solutions.21: 3 more squares: shade all four corners. A pattern with 4 lines of symmetry (2 diagonals, 1 vertical, 1 horizontal) must reflect one corner onto every other corner.
solutions.22: Equilateral triangle: 3 lines, 120°. Square: 4 lines, 90°. Rectangle: 2 lines, 180°. Regular pentagon: 5 lines, 72°. Circle: every line through the centre; every angle.
solutions.23: (a) 360° ÷ 4 = 90°. (b) 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°. (c) Yes. Bending all blades the same way keeps the 4 equal turns, so it still looks the same after each 90° turn.
solutions.24: (a) 3 lines. (b) 120°. (c) With a square: 4 lines and 90°. The square logo looks the same 4 times in a full turn, and the triangle logo 3 times.

(c) From there, which single card takes the player to +5? Which single card takes the player to −10? Can a card with a number of at most 6 take the player to +5 in one move? [2]

papers.caseStudy: In a game on a number line from −10 to +10, a player starts at 0. A green card means 'move right' and a red card means 'move left' by the number on the card.

solutions.18: (a) −7 + 3 = −4, so the blank is +4. (b) +9 − 4 = +5, so the blank is −5.
solutions.19: If the numbers are a and b: a + b = −3 and a − b = 9. Then 2a = 6, so a = 3 and b = −6. Check: 3 + (−6) = −3 and 3 − (−6) = 9.
solutions.20: 4 tokens: 1 plus, 3 minus. 6 tokens: 2 plus, 4 minus. 8 tokens: 3 plus, 5 minus. There are always 2 more − tokens than + tokens, because each +/− pair makes 0.
solutions.23: (a) 10 floors down: −10. (b) Up: +8. Down: −8. (c) Positions: +6, −3, +2, −2. It ends at floor −2. The lowest floor reached is −3, so it never goes below −3.
solutions.24: (a) 0 + 4 − 7 = −3. (b) (+4) + (−7) = −3. (c) To +5: green 8. To −10: red 7. No: from −3 to +5 is a move of 8 to the right, which needs a card of 8.
